Chapter 9: Personal Transformation—How Death Work Changes the Living
Let’s talk about something truly remarkable—the way working with the dead can quietly, but deeply, transform the living.
At first, it’s subtle. You might notice a shift in how you see things—a new appreciation for small, everyday moments, or a stronger sense of empathy that creeps in almost unnoticed. But as time goes on, those changes don’t just fade into the background—they shape everything.
Picture this: there’s a staff member who’s spent years in this world. One day, she realizes she’s noticing things she never gave a second thought to before—the gentle warmth of sunlight on her face, the sound of laughter drifting from another room, even the comfort in her daily routines.
This work has taught her to really pay attention, to savor the present, and let go of old grudges and regrets. Suddenly, life feels more precious, more fragile, and honestly, more worth living.
Relationships change, too. The staff gets used to talking about death with friends and family—those conversations most people tend to avoid. Some folks get uncomfortable, unsure of what to say. But others? They’re relieved. Grateful, even, to finally have someone who can listen without judgment. This work turns into a kind of bridge, connecting people on a much deeper level.
Now, I won’t pretend it’s all easy. There are days when the sadness feels almost too much, moments when doubt creeps in, and the weight of so many losses feels heavy.
But even then, there’s this powerful sense of purpose. The staff finds meaning in the pain—they learn how to offer comfort, how to truly be there for others during their darkest times.
Little by little, these changes become part of who they are. The work shapes their values, their priorities, even how they see themselves.
They become more patient, more compassionate, more willing to face life’s hard truths head-on. And that’s the heart of it—it’s not just about death. It’s about what it means to really live, to love, to lose, and to keep moving forward.
So, what’s the real gift here? It’s the personal transformation that comes from this work. It’s hard-won, no doubt, but so deeply rewarding.
Even in the face of loss, there’s hope, connection, and a real chance to grow. The staff carries these lessons from the crematory into every part of their lives—learning to live with more honesty, courage, and compassion than they ever thought possible.
